title: CTEs — WITH Clause
subtitle: Common Table Expressions for readable, reusable query logic
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Complex queries with nested subqueries become unreadable — a derived table inside a derived table inside a subquery. Maintenance becomes a nightmare.
whyItExists.solution: A CTE (Common Table Expression) lets you name a subquery at the top with WITH, then reference it by name in the main query. It reads like 'first compute X, then compute Y using X, then the final result.'
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any complex query with multiple steps. When you'd otherwise repeat a subquery. When you want to break a hard query into readable named parts. Recursive queries (trees, hierarchies).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For very simple queries — a CTE adds visual overhead for no benefit. In some databases, CTEs are optimization fences (not inlined) — use WITH ... AS NOT MATERIALIZED to hint the optimizer.

explainModes.beginner: A CTE is like giving a temporary name to a subquery. Instead of nesting subqueries inside each other (hard to read), you name each step at the top: WITH step1 AS (...), step2 AS (...) SELECT ... FROM step2.
explainModes.simple: WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM name. Multiple CTEs: WITH a AS (...), b AS (... FROM a ...) SELECT ... FROM b. Recursive CTE: WITH RECURSIVE generates sequences, hierarchies. Read CTEs top-to-bottom — each one can reference previous ones.
explainModes.standard: CTEs are syntactic sugar — they're evaluated like derived tables (subqueries in FROM). The optimizer may or may not inline them depending on the database and complexity. In PostgreSQL, WITH is by default an optimization fence (materialized) — use AS NOT MATERIALIZED. In SQLite, CTEs are always inlined. Multiple CTEs separated by commas, each can reference previously defined CTEs.
explainModes.technical: Recursive CTEs: WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base_case UNION ALL recursive_case). Used for: hierarchies (org chart, file tree), path generation, series generation. The recursive part references the CTE itself. Execution: 1. Evaluate base case. 2. Feed result into recursive case. 3. UNION ALL results. 4. Repeat until recursive case produces no rows. CYCLE detection available in PostgreSQL 14+ (CYCLE col SET is_cycle TO true DEFAULT false).
explainModes.deepDive: Recursive CTEs implement fixed-point computation — they keep iterating until convergence. Useful for graph traversal, bill-of-materials explosion, Fibonacci, date series. With MAXRECURSION hint (SQL Server) or LIMIT in PostgreSQL to prevent infinite loops. In PostgreSQL, WITH MATERIALIZED vs AS NOT MATERIALIZED controls whether the CTE result is computed once and stored, or re-evaluated wherever used. Modern SQL style: complex queries as a chain of named CTEs, ending in the final SELECT.

content.code:
-- Simple CTE: name a subquery
WITH high_value_orders AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM orders
    WHERE total > 1000
)
SELECT u.name, h.total, h.ordered_at
FROM high_value_orders h
JOIN users u ON h.user_id = u.id;

-- Multiple CTEs chained
WITH
order_stats AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        COUNT(*)        AS order_count,
        SUM(total)      AS total_spent,
        ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY user_id
),
top_customers AS (
    SELECT * FROM order_stats
    WHERE total_spent > 1000
)
SELECT
    u.name,
    tc.order_count,
    tc.total_spent,
    tc.avg_order
FROM top_customers tc
JOIN users u ON tc.user_id = u.id
ORDER BY tc.total_spent DESC;

-- Generate a number series 1 to 10
WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n          -- base case
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1           -- recursive case
    FROM numbers
    WHERE n < 10           -- stop condition!
)
SELECT n FROM numbers;

-- Generate dates for the next 7 days
WITH RECURSIVE dates AS (
    SELECT DATE('2024-06-01') AS d
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATE(d, '+1 day')
    FROM dates
    WHERE d < DATE('2024-06-07')
)
SELECT d FROM dates;

-- Hierarchy: employee → manager chain
-- (if we had an employees table with manager_id)
-- WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
--     SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
--     FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
--     UNION ALL
--     SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, org.depth + 1
--     FROM employees e JOIN org ON e.manager_id = org.id
-- )
-- SELECT * FROM org ORDER BY depth, name;

questions.question: What is the main advantage of CTEs over nested subqueries?
options: CTEs can be referenced multiple times in the same query
Readability — CTEs name each step, making complex queries understandable
questions.explanation: The primary advantage is readability and maintainability. A chain of named CTEs reads like a recipe: 'first compute order_stats, then find top_customers from that, then join with users.' Nested subqueries achieve the same result but become hard to read and modify. CTEs can also be referenced multiple times (a bonus over subqueries) and support recursive queries.

faq.q: Can a CTE reference another CTE defined above it?
faq.a: Yes! CTEs are defined in order and each one can reference any CTE defined before it in the same WITH clause. This is how you chain steps: WITH a AS (...), b AS (... FROM a ...), c AS (... FROM b ...) SELECT ... FROM c.

examples: WITH date_series AS (recursive date CTE) LEFT JOIN orders — fill gaps in daily order reports
WITH category_stats AS (...), above_avg AS (...) — multi-step analysis
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (...) — traverse employee hierarchy
